THE FOUR QUESTIONS
------------------
Every note answers the same four, in this order. Keeping the shape fixed is what
makes these cheap to write: the decision each time is what to say, never what
kind of piece this is.

  1. What was the problem?   The data would not answer the question as it stood.
                             State it concretely enough that a reader who has
                             never opened this dataset can feel the difficulty.
  2. What was the fix?       The construction, restriction, or design choice.
                             Enough detail to be reproduced, not the full
                             appendix.
  3. What did it cost?       Every fix drops observations, narrows the estimand,
                             or buys precision with an assumption. Say which.
                             This is the paragraph most summaries omit, and the
                             reason to read a note rather than the abstract.
  4. Does it travel?         Would it work on PODES, Susenas, Sakernas, or
                             Indonesian administrative data more broadly? This
                             is the paragraph only you can write.

LENGTH: 900–1,200 words. A note, not an essay.

TWO RULES
---------
- Do not reproduce figures or tables from the paper. Describe them, link to the
  original, and build your own exhibit from your own data if one is needed.
- Write about the technique, not the verdict. No paper is graded here.
-->
